claim: PILLAR 1, INDO-IRANIAN COMPARISON. What it is: Vedic and Avestan are close enough that the interval since their separation must be short. What it supports: a RELATIVE statement - the Rigveda is near the Indo-Iranian split - and no absolute year on its own. To yield a year it must be anchored to a dated Iranian point, which is pillar 4.
locator: Zimmer 1995, abstract via SRC-101: the two 'are so closely related that they may safely be regarded as mere dialects of a common language'; Antia 2022 reports Kellens as calling the Gathic text 'the eleventh Mandala of the Rigveda, only written in a slightly different dialect'
notes: Abstract level only; neither work was read. The argument's form is a rate assumption - that languages this similar cannot have been apart long - and no retrieved source in this record states or defends a rate. That gap is the pillar's weakest joint and it is not closed here.

claim: PILLAR 2, THE MITANNI TERMS AS TERMINUS ANTE QUEM. What it is: Indo-Aryan divine names and technical vocabulary in Hurrian-language documents of northern Mesopotamia, conventionally c.1500-1300 BCE. What it supports: that Indo-Aryan language existed by c.1400 BCE. It does NOT by itself support any date for the Rigveda, because the Mitanni material is not the Rigveda and may be earlier than, later than, or contemporary with it.
locator: SRC-107, Macdonell introduction, on the 1907 discovery: 'the phonetic form in which these names there appear may quite well belong to the Indo-Iranian period when the Indians and the Persians were still one people'; SRC-108, Sayce 1909 JRAS, arguing from the same tablet that Indic and Iranian developed contemporaneously over a wide area; SRC-106, Parpola 2015 ch.9 abstract, 'The Rigvedic language is slightly younger than Mitanni Indo-Aryan of c. 1500-1300 bce'
notes: The three retrieved readings of ONE body of evidence are incompatible: Macdonell reads the Mitanni forms as pre-dating the Indo-Iranian split and therefore as constraining nothing; Sayce reads them as contemporary with a wide Aryan area; Parpola reads them as a stage the Rigvedic language is slightly younger than. The disagreement is 1909-2015 and unresolved. Calling this a terminus ante quem states a conclusion, not the evidence.

claim: PILLAR 3, THE ABSENCE OF IRON. What it is: the Rigveda is said to describe no iron, and iron becomes common in South Asia in the earlier first millennium BCE, so the text is earlier. What it supports: NOTHING, until the absence is typed and the semantic question about ayas- is settled. Neither has been done in this repository.
locator: SRC-113, Erb-Satullo 2019 abstract: the first major expansion of iron 'occurred in the late second and early first millennium BC' - in the Near East, not South Asia; SRC-116, the 1915 Nature notice of Neogi, who 'advances evidence, chiefly based on the Rigveda, in favour of the view that iron was known and used between 2000 and 1000 B.C.'; SRC-115, Semenenko 2019 abstract, running the same argument form over swords to a date 'prior to 2600 BC'
notes: Three faults, each independently disabling. First, the premise is contested and has been since 1915 (SRC-116). Second, the comparison chronology retrieved here is Near Eastern, not South Asian (SRC-113). Third, the argument form does not constrain the answer: SRC-115 runs it over the same corpus and reaches a date roughly 1,300 years earlier than the conventional one. This record adopts neither date. The lemma ayas- is the whole question and is untouched: PUR4J-012 records ayasa- 'of metal' in 8 pur- passages without deciding which metal.

claim: PILLAR 4, AVESTAN PARALLELS. What it is: the Gathas and the Rigveda share formulae, metre, deities and ritual, so their dates are close. What it supports: whatever date the Gathas are assigned, plus or minus the closeness. It transmits the Gathic uncertainty rather than removing it, and the retrieved Gathic dates span roughly 750 years.
locator: SRC-109, Burrow 1979 JRAS snippet: the Gathas 'seems now likely to be between 1100 and 1000 before our era', citing Shahbazi BSOAS XL (1977) 25-35; SRC-110, Irannejad 2022 abstract, placing the Old Avestan texts in 'the second quarter of the second millennium BCE', i.e. c.1750-1500 BCE; SRC-111, Brereton and Jamison 2020 ch. 'Historical Context', abstract, which compares the two corpora and states no absolute date
notes: The retrieved spread for the Gathas alone is c.1750 BCE to c.1000 BCE. A Rigvedic date computed through this pillar cannot be tighter than that spread, and every published point estimate that uses it is tighter. Shahbazi 1977, the work Burrow's date rests on, is not retrieved. Zoroaster's date is a live dispute in Iranian studies and this record does not enter it.

claim: PILLAR 5, THE STACKED INTERVAL. Not on the brief's list, and it is the pillar that actually carries the conventional figure in the source where the argument is set out in full. Form: Buddhism spreads c.500 BCE; it presupposes the Brahmanas and Upanisads; those require seven or eight centuries of development; therefore the oldest hymns are no later than the thirteenth century BCE.
locator: SRC-107, Macdonell introduction, verbatim: 'The development of language and religious [th]ought apparent in the extensive literature of the successive phases of these two Vedic periods renders it necessary to postulate the lapse of seven or eight centuries'; SRC-114, Elby 2014, Religion Compass 8:128-138, chunk 4, giving Proferes' Brahmana date of 'roughly 1100 BCE' and chunk 1, that composition 'is likely to have continued for almost a millennium' with 'not a neat temporal progression between the different categories of text'
notes: The seven-or-eight-century interval is an estimate of how long linguistic and religious change takes. It is not measured, and no retrieved source measures it. It is also the largest single term in the sum. The 500 BCE Buddhist anchor is not sourced anywhere in this repository (DA-D-006 note). Elby's 'not a neat temporal progression' cuts directly against the stacking.

claim: WHAT THE FOUR PILLARS TOGETHER SUPPORT. Taking only what the retrieved sources state, the defensible statement is a RANGE and not a point: the Rigveda was composed over an extended period ending somewhere in the second half of the second millennium BCE, with the retrieved positions spanning roughly 1750-1000 BCE for its Iranian anchor and roughly 1300-1200 BCE for one explicit proposal about the Rigveda itself.
locator: the four pillar rows above, taken together; no single retrieved source states this range
notes: Stated as a range because that is what the evidence retrieved here supports, and stated as PROVISIONAL because every input is an abstract or a snippet and none was read in full. Two things this row does NOT say: it does not endorse a point estimate, and it does not exclude proposals outside the range - it records that nothing retrieved here supports one. The range is wide, it is honestly wide, and narrowing it is a retrieval problem, not an argument problem.

claim: THE CONVENTIONAL DATE IS INFERRED, NOT ATTESTED, AND ITS INFERENCE CHAIN HAS NO INDEPENDENT LEG. Pillar 1 yields no year without pillar 4; pillar 4 inherits the Gathic dispute; pillar 2 is read three incompatible ways by the three retrieved sources; pillar 3 fails its own premise; pillar 5 turns on an unmeasured interval. No pillar reaches a year on its own.
locator: DA-C-001 to DA-C-005, each with its own sources
notes: This is a statement about the structure of the argument, not a claim that the conventional date is wrong. It may well be right. What this record establishes is that this repository cannot presently say WHY it is right, and must therefore not write it as though it were an observation.
